title: Interstitial Lung Disease
subject: Medicine
summary: A group of >200 disorders causing inflammation or fibrosis of the lung interstitium, presenting with dry cough and dyspnoea. Diagnosis relies on history, exam, imaging and limited tests, often in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: ILD refers to any disease that primarily involves the lung interstitium, leading to impaired gas exchange. Diagnosis requires a compatible clinical picture, exclusion of alternative causes, and evidence of interstitial involvement on imaging or pathology.
b: Dry, persistent cough and progressive dyspnoea are typical.
Chest X‑ray showing reticular pattern or honey‑comb in advanced disease.
High‑resolution CT (HRCT) is the gold standard; look for ground‑glass opacities, reticulation, traction bronchiectasis.

t.b: Does the film show interstitial pattern? → Positive suggests ILD; normal does not exclude early disease.
What pattern is present? → Ground‑glass = inflammation; reticulation/honey‑comb = fibrosis; guides management.
Is there a restrictive defect? → Reduced FVC with normal or high FEV1/FVC supports ILD.
Are there treatable triggers? → Positive HIV or TB directs specific therapy.

sections.p: Severity is graded by physiologic impairment and radiologic extent. The GAP index (Gender, Age, Physiology) is practical even without CT quantification.
b: Stage I: FVC ≥ 80 % predicted, DLCO ≥ 55 % predicted.
Stage II: FVC 50‑79 %, DLCO 40‑54 %.
Stage III: FVC < 50 % or DLCO < 40 %.

t.b: How much lung volume is lost? → Guides prognosis and transplant referral.
Is gas transfer severely reduced? → Low DLCO predicts higher mortality.

sections.p: In low‑resource East African hospitals, the commonest triggers are infections and environmental exposures, followed by connective‑tissue disease and drug toxicity.
b: Post‑TB sequelae (fibrotic change after pulmonary TB).
HIV‑associated pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia leading to organising pneumonia.
Silica dust from mining or stone‑cutting.
Chronic exposure to biomass smoke (cooking with firewood).
Drug‑induced (e.g., anti‑TB drugs, antiretrovirals, herbal remedies).
Autoimmune (systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis) – less common but important.

sections.p: Patients usually present with a dry, non‑productive cough and exertional dyspnoea. Early disease may have normal auscultation; later stages show fine “Velcro” crackles and digital clubbing.
b: Cough: dry, persistent, worse at night.
Dyspnoea: progressive, limits walking > 100 m.
Auscultation: fine inspiratory crackles at bases.
Clubbing: present in > 30 % of chronic cases.

sections.p: Select tests that answer the key clinical questions while recognising limited resources.

t.b: Is there an interstitial pattern? → Positive supports ILD; normal does not rule out early disease.
What is the radiologic pattern? → Guides specific diagnosis (e.g., organising pneumonia vs. usual interstitial pneumonia).
What is the functional severity? → Restrictive defect with reduced DLCO confirms physiologic impact.
Are treatable infections present? → Positive results direct antimicrobial therapy.
Is a connective‑tissue disease driving ILD? → Positive results prompt rheumatology referral.

t.a: Bronchoscopy with BAL – only if severe and facilities exist
t.b: Is there an infection or alveolar hemorrhage? → Guides targeted treatment.

sections.p: Identify features that signal rapid progression or life‑threatening complications.
b: Rapid decline in FVC > 10 % in 3 months.
New onset hypoxaemia at rest (SpO₂ < 88 %).
Development of pulmonary hypertension (echo shows RV pressure > 35 mmHg).
Acute exacerbation: sudden worsening dyspnoea, new infiltrates.

sections.p: Treat the underlying trigger, then provide anti‑fibrotic or anti‑inflammatory therapy and supportive care.
b: Remove exposure (stop smoking, avoid silica, improve ventilation).
If post‑TB or infection: complete antimicrobial course.
Corticosteroids (prednisone) for organising pneumonia, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, or acute exacerbation – start high dose then taper.
Anti‑fibrotic agents (pirfenidone, nintedanib) where available; avoid if severe liver disease.
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus.
Long‑term oxygen if PaO₂ < 55 mmHg or SpO₂ < 88 % on room air.
Pulmonary rehabilitation to improve exercise tolerance.

sections.p: Regular monitoring detects progression early; prevention focuses on exposure control and vaccination.
b: Clinic review every 3‑6 months with spirometry and symptom questionnaire.
Repeat HRCT only if clinical change suggests a new pattern.
Educate patients on avoiding biomass smoke and smoking cessation.
Screen household contacts for TB if post‑TB ILD.

sections.p: Conditions that share cough and crackles can mislead clinicians.
b: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease – has productive cough, wheeze, and obstructive spirometry.
Congestive heart failure – presents with dyspnoea but has basal crackles, peripheral oedema, and elevated BNP.
Pulmonary tuberculosis – may have cavitary lesions and systemic symptoms; sputum positive.

sections.p: Beware of false‑negative or non‑specific findings.
b: Normal chest X‑ray early in disease; rely on HRCT if suspicion high.
Spirometry may appear normal if testing is poor; repeat if symptoms progress.
HIV test window period – repeat if recent exposure.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening of breathlessness with SpO₂ < 88 % or new chest pain.
Rapid fall in lung function (>10 % FVC in 3 months).
Signs of right‑heart failure (ankle swelling, jugular venous distension).

faq.q: Why is the cough usually dry in ILD?
faq.a: Inflammation/fibrosis is in the interstitium, not the airways, so mucus production is minimal.

faq.q: Can a patient with ILD live without oxygen?
faq.a: If resting SpO₂ stays ≥ 88 % and exercise desaturation is mild, long‑term oxygen may not be needed initially.
Only when infection or malignancy is suspected and imaging is non‑diagnostic; otherwise HRCT plus clinical context is sufficient.

exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer with progressive dyspnoea and fine crackles – what is your next diagnostic step and why? — Obtain HRCT to characterise the interstitial pattern because chest X‑ray is often non‑specific.

A patient with known HIV presents with dry cough and new ground‑glass opacities – which reversible cause should you consider first? — Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia; treat with TMP‑SMX and reassess.
Why are corticosteroids contraindicated in usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern? — UIP is fibrotic; steroids have little benefit and increase infection risk.
What exposure history is most relevant in East African patients with ILD? — Silica dust from mining, biomass smoke from cooking, and post‑TB scarring.
How does the GAP index influence management decisions? — Higher GAP stage predicts mortality and may prompt early transplant referral or aggressive anti‑fibrotic therapy.
A patient on anti‑TB therapy develops acute dyspnoea and diffuse infiltrates – what drug toxicity should you suspect? — Rifampicin‑induced interstitial lung disease; stop the offending drug.
What are the red‑flag features indicating an acute exacerbation of ILD? — Rapid worsening dyspnoea, new bilateral infiltrates, and hypoxaemia without infection.
Explain why long‑term oxygen improves survival in ILD. — It corrects chronic hypoxaemia, reduces pulmonary hypertension, and improves exercise capacity.
